Working with Product Marketing

Decision rights, claim liability, and what the handoff really transfers
Assumes the working-knowledge treatment of this topic: the four-step handoff, launch tiering, the RACI, and the vocabulary of positioning versus messaging. This page argues with that material rather than repeating it.

At 7.40 on the morning of Tuesday 3 November 2026, Sandhya Balakrishnan opened a Slack thread that had been running since 11 the previous night and understood, with the particular clarity that arrives before coffee, that her launch had a problem no process would solve. Kolam Labs, where she had been a product manager for two years, sold an agentic document-processing product to Indian lenders and insurers: point a Kolam agent at a folder of loan files and it extracted, cross-checked and flagged the twenty-two fields an underwriter actually reads. Two hundred and six paying accounts, a self-serve tier that had grown to 41 per cent of new logos, and an enterprise motion that closed three or four deals a quarter at an average of ₹62 lakh. The launch of Kolam Verify — the product's first genuinely autonomous review mode, in which the agent did not merely extract but adjudicated, marking a file clear or held — was nineteen days away. Everything the handbook required had been done. Meera Kuruvilla, the product marketing lead, had been in the room since the first problem brief in July. The positioning had been argued through and settled in August. Sales had been certified in October. The battlecard existed. The webinar had four hundred registrations.

The problem in the thread was that the number had moved. The enablement deck, the landing page, the pricing model and two signed pilot agreements all rested on a single sentence — Kolam Verify clears 94 per cent of standard retail loan files without human review — and the infrastructure team had upgraded the underlying model on 28 October, three days earlier, as part of a routine monthly refresh that no one had thought to put on the launch calendar. On Kolam's internal benchmark the new model was better: 95.8 per cent, up from 94.1. On the document mix of the two largest pilot customers, both of whom used regional-language addendum pages, it was worse: 89.6 per cent. The claim that had been certified into forty-one salespeople, written into a pricing page and repeated in a press briefing scheduled for the following Monday was now, depending on whose files you ran it against, either conservative or false. Nobody had been negligent. The handoff had been textbook. And the artefact that mattered most — the claim — had no owner, no version number, and no re-certification date.

Eleven hundred kilometres away in Pune, Arvind Ramanathan had a different version of the same problem, and a harder one, because his was printed. Kanthi Diagnostics manufactured a point-of-care haematology analyser — a shoebox-sized instrument with a cartridge, a touchscreen and a cloud service that pushed results into hospital information systems. Kanthi sold to diagnostic-lab chains and to the 200-to-600-bed private hospital segment, through a mix of direct sales in eight cities and forty-one channel partners everywhere else. Arvind's launch was the Kanthi K2, a second-generation instrument whose real advance was not in the optics but in the software: an on-device quality-control routine that reduced the daily calibration burden from roughly eighteen minutes of a technician's time to under four. The commercial argument wrote itself, and Priyanka Deshmukh, Kanthi's product marketing manager, had written it: fourteen minutes back, every morning, on every instrument.

Arvind's difficulty was that the packaging carton, the printed quick-start guide and the channel-partner catalogue insert went to press on 6 October for a 12 February launch — a hundred and thirty days of lead time driven by a printer in Vasai, a carton design that had to carry regulatory text, and a channel that ordered in January for the financial-year-end buying season. The software feature that justified the claim was not finished on 6 October. It was scheduled to be finished on 20 December, and the on-device QC routine's performance against the three cartridge lots then in production was, in the firmware team's own words, "trending well". Twenty-two thousand cartons, ₹41 lakh of print, and a claim that would be physically unretractable the moment the pallets left Vasai. Priyanka had asked Arvind a question in September that he had not been able to answer and that had bothered him ever since: if this number turns out to be nine minutes instead of fourteen, who apologises?

These two situations look like different problems — a model refresh and a printing deadline — and are in fact the same problem seen from two ends. In both cases the process of the handoff was done correctly and the substance of the handoff was left unowned. That gap is the subject of this page. The argument it will make, and then test against edge cases, disagreements and failure modes, is this: the PM–PMM handoff does not transfer work, and it does not really transfer documents. It allocates decision rights over a set of claims about the world, most of which are perishable, several of which are irreversible, and none of which has a natural owner. Everything useful in the discipline — tiering, RACIs, enablement, win-loss, the eight-week runway — is downstream of that allocation, and every durable failure is a failure of it.

1 The idea, stated precisely, and where it came from

Begin with a definition sharp enough to argue with. Product marketing is the function accountable for the claims a company makes about a product in the market, and for the capability of every customer-facing surface to make those claims accurately and consistently. A claim, in this usage, is any assertion about the product that a buyer could act on and later find false: what it does, who it is for, what it costs, what it replaces, what it outperforms, how much it saves, what it will not do. Positioning is the selection of the frame in which claims are evaluated. Messaging is the rendering of claims into language. Enablement is the distribution of claims to the humans who will repeat them. Pricing is a claim about value expressed in currency. Under this definition the PM–PMM handoff is the moment at which authorship of claims passes from the person who knows what the product does to the person accountable for what the market is told it does, and the whole art lies in the fact that those two knowledge sets never fully overlap.

This framing is unfashionable because it sounds narrow. It is in fact the widest available framing, because a claim implies a claimant, a truth condition and a decay rate, and those three properties generate almost every mechanic the discipline has invented. Sandhya's problem was a claim whose truth condition was model-dependent and whose decay rate turned out to be monthly. Arvind's was a claim whose truth condition was firmware-dependent and whose reversibility had been surrendered to a printing press in Vasai a hundred and thirty days before anyone would know the answer.

The split is an accident of specialisation, not a law of nature

The intellectual history matters here in a way it does not for most process topics, because the two roles began as one and the arguments about the handoff are, almost without exception, arguments about whether the separation was worth it. In May 1931 Neil McElroy, a promotions manager at Procter & Gamble in Cincinnati, wrote a three-page memo proposing what became the brand-man system: a single named person responsible for a brand's profit, its product, its advertising, its packaging and its field support, with a small team reporting to him. McElroy's brand man owned the product and the market simultaneously, and that co-ownership was the point of the design; the memo's force came from arguing that split responsibility for a brand produced no responsibility at all. Both modern roles descend from that memo, and both inherit its logic, which is why each can quote scripture at the other.

The split came later and came from technology. As computing products acquired long engineering cycles and genuine technical complexity through the 1970s and 1980s, firms like Hewlett-Packard and IBM found that the person who could hold a specification in their head and the person who could hold a channel in their head were rarely the same person, and formalised a division between a technically-oriented product manager and an outward-facing product marketing manager. Regis McKenna, writing from Silicon Valley in the 1980s and most famously in his 1991 Harvard Business Review essay "Marketing Is Everything", pushed hard against the idea that this meant marketing came second: in his account, in markets where technology changes faster than customers' mental models, the positioning of a product is a design input rather than a downstream description. Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm (1991) gave that instinct an operational template. The Pragmatic Institute, founded in 1993, then did something less glamorous and arguably more consequential: it drew the boxes. Its framework enumerates several dozen discrete activities — market problems, win-loss analysis, pricing, buyer personas, launch plan, sales enablement, channel training — and assigns each to product management or to marketing, which converted a philosophical question into an org-design checklist that thousands of companies adopted wholesale. April Dunford's Obviously Awesome (2019) then re-radicalised the upstream claim for the SaaS era, arguing that positioning is a set of deliberate choices about competitive alternatives and market category that precede messaging and often precede the roadmap.

Running against that whole lineage is the empowered-team tradition associated with Marty Cagan and the Silicon Valley Product Group, which holds that a cross-functional product team must be accountable for outcomes, not output, and that business viability — whether the thing can be sold, at what price, through what channel, with what claims — is one of the four risks the team itself must resolve before building, with product marketing as an indispensable contributor rather than a receiving party. In its strong form this position denies that a handoff should exist at all: if there is a moment at which the product becomes someone else's problem, the team was never accountable for the outcome in the first place.

The schools, and the propositions each will and will not sign

It is worth being exact about who disagrees with whom, because in practice these positions are held by intelligent people inside the same company, usually without anyone naming them, and a PM who can name them can referee the argument instead of losing it.

The revenue-enablement school grew up where a single mis-briefed rep could cost a quarter. Asking which school is correct in the abstract is the wrong question; the productive question is which environment you are in, and the rest of this page is largely an attempt to make that question answerable.

Why the economics point the same way

There is a cleaner way to see the disagreement, borrowed from the economics of organisation. Michael Jensen and William Meckling's treatment of decision rights argues that authority should sit where the relevant knowledge is, because knowledge is expensive to move and authority is cheap to move; where knowledge is specific — costly to transfer, tacit, held in one person's head — you move the decision to the knowledge. Where it is general — codifiable, transferable in a document — you may move the knowledge to the decision-maker instead. Apply that test artefact by artefact and the PM–PMM boundary stops being a matter of taste. The failure rate of an extraction model on regional-language addendum pages is specific knowledge sitting with Sandhya's team; no brief will transfer it faithfully, so the decision about what may be claimed regarding accuracy must sit with, or be jointly signed by, the people who hold it. The willingness of a 400-bed hospital's procurement committee to pay a premium for technician-minutes is specific knowledge sitting with Priyanka and her channel partners; no product spec transfers it, so the packaging and price decision must sit there. The interesting artefacts are the ones where the knowledge is split — naming, pricing, the accuracy claim — and those, predictably, are exactly the artefacts that go wrong.

The sentence a senior PM should be able to say in a room of executives: "The handoff is not when marketing gets told. It is when we decide, artefact by artefact, who signs the claim, how we would know it had become false, and what it costs us to take it back."

2 Mechanics in depth: the three things the handoff actually moves

Practitioners who are good at this do three things that are almost never written down, and each has second-order consequences that explain behaviour otherwise hard to account for. They map artefacts by reversibility and by where the knowledge lives; they run a claim ledger with explicit decay; and they manage product marketing as a queue rather than as a calendar. Take them in order.

2.1 The reversibility map

The standard handoff artefact list — positioning statement, messaging framework, battlecard, pricing sheet, launch plan — is organised by document type, which is the least useful possible axis, because it tells you nothing about what happens when you are wrong. Expert teams organise the same list on two axes: how expensive the artefact is to reverse, and whether the knowledge needed to get it right is product-side or market-side. The resulting map tells you both who should hold the pen and how much evidence you should demand before the pen moves.

The map makes a prediction that holds up well against experience: the artefacts organisations write the most process about are the cheap-to-reverse ones, because those are the ones that generate frequent, visible, low-stakes friction — who edits the landing page, who approves the email — while the expensive ones generate rare, catastrophic, low-frequency friction and therefore never accumulate enough incidents to justify a procedure. Naming is the clearest instance. A product name propagates into the repository, the billing system, the API namespace, the support macro library, the documentation URL structure, the partner catalogue and the customers' own internal wikis; changing it eighteen months later is a six-figure exercise in most B2B companies and a brand event in consumer. It is also, in the median company, decided by whoever created the Jira epic. Ask a PM who named their last three features and roughly half will say an engineer did, without embarrassment, because naming does not feel like a claim. It is a claim — specifically, a claim about which category the thing belongs to, and therefore about what a buyer will compare it with.

2.2 The claim ledger, with worked arithmetic

The second practice is the one that would have saved both protagonists, and it is simple enough to be embarrassing: a list of the claims the launch will make, each with a named signatory, a truth condition expressed as something measurable, a falsification probability, a retraction cost, and a re-check date. Call it the claim ledger. The arithmetic is expected-cost-of-error, done per claim rather than per launch.

Work Kanthi's through, because the numbers are concrete. Priyanka and Arvind sat down on 24 September with four candidate claims for the K2 and priced each one. The retraction cost is not a guess; it is the sum of the specific things that must happen if the claim proves false, and the discipline of enumerating those things is most of the value.

First, the claim everybody was proudest of — the fourteen minutes — carried 72 per cent of the expected cost, entirely because its falsification probability was high, not because its retraction cost was the largest. Second, the claim with the highest retraction cost, cartridge backward compatibility at ₹96 lakh, was barely discussed before the exercise, because it was considered a technical fact rather than a marketing claim; it was in fact both, and the insight that a spec line printed on a carton becomes a claim the moment a channel partner repeats it is exactly the kind of thing the ledger surfaces. Third, and most usefully, the ledger reframes the printing deadline. The question is no longer "can we hit 6 October", it is "which claims can survive being frozen on 6 October", and those are different questions with different answers. The formal version, for readers who want it, is unremarkable but worth stating: for claim i, expected cost of error Ei = pi × Ci, where Ci scales with the substrate's reversal cost and with the number of downstream repetitions before correction. Since repetitions accumulate over time, a claim's total exposure is better modelled as pi × c × r × t, where r is repetitions per week and t is weeks to detection. This is why detection latency, not falsification probability, is usually the cheapest variable to attack: Kolam could not make the model stop changing, but it could make the gap between a model change and a claim re-check shrink from "whenever someone notices" to seven days, which reduced exposure by roughly the same factor as halving the error rate would have.

2.3 Message fidelity decays multiplicatively

The third mechanic is the one most often mistaken for a training problem. When a company complains that four salespeople describe a feature four different ways, the reflex is to run more enablement. The structure of the problem says otherwise. A claim passes through a chain of human relays — PMM writes it, a regional sales manager re-teaches it in a Monday call, a rep internalises it, the rep says it to a buyer, the buyer repeats it to their own committee — and at each relay some fidelity is lost. If each relay preserves a fraction r of the intended meaning, fidelity after n relays is rn, which falls off a cliff faster than intuition expects.

Meera Kuruvilla's test at Kolam was blunt: she pulled six reps at random a fortnight after certification and asked each to write the claim on paper. When four of six produced something she would have let a customer hear, she considered the enablement complete. When it was three, she did not run another session; she shortened the sentence.

2.4 Product marketing is a queue, not a calendar

The standard advice — bring product marketing in eight to ten weeks before launch — is good advice that fails in a specific and common way, and the failure is instructive because it looks like a discipline problem and is actually a capacity problem. Product marketing teams are small. A four-person PMM function supporting an engineering organisation that ships eleven notable releases a quarter is not late because it is disorganised; it is late because it is a service system operating above the utilisation at which queues stay short.

The arithmetic is standard queueing theory and worth doing once. By Little's Law, average work-in-progress L equals arrival rate λ times average time in system W. Kolam's PMM team was three people; a full-tier launch consumed roughly six weeks of elapsed PMM involvement, and each PMM could genuinely hold two launches concurrently, giving L = 6 and a sustainable arrival rate of λ = L/W = 6/6 = one launch per week, or thirteen a quarter. Engineering at Kolam shipped nine releases a quarter that the teams considered launch-worthy, which looks comfortable until you notice that PMM also owned competitive research, two analyst relationships, quarterly pricing review and the customer-reference programme, which together consumed about 40 per cent of capacity. Effective launch capacity was therefore nearer eight a quarter against nine arrivals — utilisation ρ ≈ 0.89 — and at that utilisation the expected queue wait scales roughly as ρ/(1 − ρ), which is about eight units of service time. In plain terms: at 89 per cent utilisation a launch that needs six weeks of PMM attention waits far longer than six weeks to get it, and the waiting is invisible because nobody logs it.

This reframes launch tiering entirely. Tiering is usually taught as a way to right-size investment per launch. Its deeper function is admission control on a queue: it is the mechanism by which an organisation decides what not to admit, so that utilisation stays in the region where the system responds. A tiering scheme that classifies 70 per cent of releases as top tier has not right-sized anything; it has abolished admission control and guaranteed that the launches that matter will be served by an exhausted team. The tell is easy to check and rarely checked: count the proportion of releases in the top tier over the last four quarters. If it exceeds about a quarter of them, the scheme is decorative.

3 When the model applies, when it does not, and when it actively misleads

The claims-and-decision-rights model advanced here is not universally applicable, and a practitioner who applies it everywhere will be wrong in predictable places. Its conditions can be stated as testable claims, and it is worth applying each to both protagonists rather than leaving them abstract.

Condition one: claims are costly to retract. The model earns its keep where a false claim imposes real cost — refunds, regulatory attention, channel credibility, a printed carton. Test: can you name, in rupees, what it costs to take back the central claim of your last launch? Kanthi could and did: ₹74 lakh on the fourteen-minute claim, which is why the ledger changed the plan. Kolam's case was subtler, because software claims feel retractable; a landing page is edited in ten minutes. But Kolam's accuracy claim had propagated into two signed pilot agreements with a service-level clause, which converted a soft claim into a contractual one, and the retraction cost was therefore not the cost of editing a page but the cost of renegotiating two contracts and the reputational cost with a lender's risk committee, a constituency with a long memory. Where retraction is genuinely cheap — a consumer app testing five value propositions in parallel on a store listing — the ledger is overhead, and the correct discipline is experimentation, not signature.

Condition two: the knowledge required is genuinely split. The model matters where no single person can hold both the product truth and the market truth. Test: can one person in the building answer both "what is the p95 latency on a 4G connection in Nashik" and "what will a 300-bed hospital's purchase committee pay for a technician-hour"? At Kanthi, plainly not. At Kolam, borderline: Meera had been close enough to the model evaluation work to ask good questions, which is exactly why she was the one who spotted, in the 3 November thread, that the benchmark figure in the deck had no date on it. In a fifteen-person startup where the founder does both jobs, the model degrades into a checklist the founder runs against themselves, which is worth doing but is not a handoff.

Condition three: claims decay. The model is most valuable where the truth condition changes without anyone deciding to change it. Software with monthly model refreshes, hardware with lot-to-lot variation, competitive claims in a market where a rival reprices quarterly: all decay. A claim about a stable, deterministic, non-comparative property — "supports Tamil" — does not, and does not need a re-check date. Kolam sat at the extreme end of this axis and had not noticed.

Condition four: there is more than one relay between the claim's author and the buyer. Where the product sells itself with no humans in the chain, the fidelity arithmetic collapses to a single link and enablement stops mattering; the landing page is the rep. This is why pure self-serve businesses can run with a much thinner product marketing function than their revenue would suggest, and why they are nonetheless not exempt: their single relay is high-stakes and highly measurable, which shifts the work from enablement to experimentation without reducing it.

Where the model actively misleads is worth stating as plainly. First, it misleads in genuinely exploratory work. A team running a two-week probe with thirty friendly users to learn whether a problem exists at all has no claims to manage, and imposing a ledger on it converts learning into theatre; the correct posture there is to make the provisionality explicit to everyone touched by the probe and then move fast. Second, it misleads when it is used to justify gatekeeping. A claim ledger in the hands of a product marketing function that reports into revenue and is measured on rep productivity becomes an instrument for blocking anything that complicates the current quarter's narrative, which is a real and documented pathology. Third, and most subtly, it misleads in category-creation situations. When a company is deliberately inventing a category, the central claim is by construction unfalsifiable at launch — there is no benchmark, no comparison, no established truth condition — and a framework built on falsifiability will systematically undervalue the most strategically important work the firm does. The honest answer there is that the ledger applies to the product's performance claims and not to the category claim, and that the category claim is governed by a different discipline entirely.

4 Hard edge cases and what happens at the organisational seams

4.1 Multi-product portfolios: the attach problem

In a single-product company the positioning question is "what is this compared to". In a portfolio it becomes "what is this compared to, including our own other products", and that second clause is where the seam opens. Consider Kinnari Enterprise Cloud, a Hyderabad firm with four products sold to the same finance-function buyer: an expense product, a procurement product, a vendor-payments product and an analytics layer. Each product has a PM. Product marketing is organised by segment, not by product, so one PMM covers all four for mid-market. When the procurement PM launches a spend-approval workflow that substantially overlaps the expense product's approval chains, the positioning decision is not hers to make and is not really the PMM's either: it is a portfolio decision about which product carries approvals, and it has revenue consequences for two P&Ls. What mature companies say they do is resolve this in a portfolio council. What they actually do, in the observable majority of cases, is let the louder PM ship first and let the field work out the story, which produces the characteristic symptom of portfolio companies — two products whose sales collateral contradicts each other, discovered by a customer rather than by the company. The structural fix, where it works, is that portfolio-level positioning is a standing artefact owned by product marketing with a named executive arbiter, refreshed quarterly, and that individual launches are checked against it rather than negotiated against each other. The reason this fix is rarer than it should be is that it requires someone senior to be accountable for a document nobody reads until it is violated.

4.2 Two-sided markets: whose launch is it

Khoj Bazaar, a services marketplace connecting households with verified home-repair professionals across nine cities, ran into the canonical version of this. A new instant-booking feature was, from the demand side, an unambiguous improvement: no waiting for a callback, a confirmed slot in ninety seconds. From the supply side it was a reduction in the professional's ability to triage jobs by travel distance and ticket size, which the better-earning professionals used deliberately. The handoff question is not who writes the copy; it is which side hears about it first, and in what frame, and that sequencing decision has a liquidity consequence the PM can quantify and the PMM cannot. Khoj's PM could model that a 6 per cent reduction in supply-side acceptance rate in a city would raise average fulfilment time past the threshold at which demand-side repeat rate fell measurably; the PMM could model that a supply-first announcement would generate organised pushback in the professionals' own informal groups within days. Both were right. The resolution Khoj reached — supply-side first, in three pilot cities, framed as guaranteed-payment-on-instant-jobs rather than as a booking change, with demand-side messaging held for four weeks — is an example of the general rule at two-sided seams: the side with the higher switching cost and the lower tolerance for surprise gets the first, most carefully framed communication, even though the side with the visible benefit is the one the company is excited about. The rule is routinely violated because demand-side launches are what get celebrated.

4.3 Regulated products: when claims have a second reader

In lending, insurance and health products, the claim ledger acquires an external auditor. Kartavya Insure, which sold a motor-claims automation platform to insurers, discovered the hard version: its marketing material described the product as deciding claims, when what it did was recommend decisions to a human assessor, and the distinction that felt like pedantry to the growth team was the entire distinction that mattered to its customers' compliance officers, several of whom were themselves accountable to the IRDAI for how claim decisions were made. The practical consequence in regulated categories is that a negative artefact becomes as important as a positive one: an explicit do-not-say list, maintained jointly, versioned, and taught alongside the battlecard. Firms that get this right treat the do-not-say list as a first-class enablement asset with its own review cadence; firms that get it wrong discover it exists only after a rep has said the forbidden thing on a recorded call. The second consequence is that the handoff gains a mandatory third party — legal or compliance — and the sequencing changes: claims are drafted by product marketing, validated by product, cleared by compliance, and only then certified into the field, which lengthens the cycle by two to four weeks and is one of the legitimate reasons regulated companies' launch runways look bloated to outsiders.

4.4 Hardware plus software: the substrate decides the schedule

Arvind's problem generalises. In hardware-plus-software businesses, the marketing artefacts have manufacturing lead times, and those lead times are set by vendors whose schedules are indifferent to the firmware backlog. The under-appreciated second-order effect is that this inverts the normal direction of the handoff: instead of product marketing waiting on product, product is forced to commit to claims before the engineering evidence exists, which is precisely the condition under which claims become fiction. The expert move, which Kanthi eventually made, is to sort claims by substrate and put only the durable ones on the irreversible surface. A related move, common among experienced hardware PMMs, is to design the printed artefact to carry categories rather than numbers — "faster daily calibration" on the carton, "fourteen minutes" on the website — accepting weaker copy on the permanent substrate in exchange for the ability to be precise on the perishable one. The third complication is the channel: forty-one partners re-state the claim in their own words, in their own languages, to customers Kanthi never meets, and each partner is an additional relay in the fidelity chain with a relay coefficient considerably below 0.85 because the partner also sells three competing instruments.

4.5 AI-native products: the claim with a shelf life

Kolam's situation is the emblematic new case and deserves the most careful treatment, because it breaks an assumption every framework in this field was built on: that the product's behaviour is stable between the writing of the claim and the buyer's experience of it. For a probabilistic system whose underlying model is updated on a schedule the product team may not control, the truth condition of a performance claim has a half-life. Three specific consequences follow. First, claims must be scoped to a stated evaluation set and a date — "94 per cent on the standard retail-loan benchmark, measured 12 September 2026" — which sales organisations hate because it is weaker copy and which is the only honest formulation available. Second, the benchmark itself becomes a jointly-owned artefact, because whoever controls the evaluation set controls the claim; at Kolam the evaluation set had been assembled by two engineers in March from whatever files were handy, which is a reasonable way to build a regression test and an indefensible way to build the basis of a commercial promise. Third, and most difficult, the handoff acquires a recurring component: not a single transfer before launch but a standing re-certification, in which product marketing is notified of model changes the way security teams are notified of dependency updates. Kolam's eventual answer was a rule that any change to a production model triggered a seven-day claim re-check before it could reach accounts covered by an accuracy commitment, which is an operational burden the company would not have accepted had it not first been surprised.

There is a further AI-specific seam that is easy to miss. The demo is the claim. In a deterministic product a demo shows what the product does; in a probabilistic one a demo shows one favourable sample from a distribution, and the gap between the demo and the buyer's first ten files is the single largest source of post-sale disappointment in this product class. Whose job is that gap? Product marketing builds the demo, so it looks like theirs. Product knows the distribution, so the knowledge is theirs. In practice the companies that handle it well require the demo script to be run against a randomly drawn sample from the same evaluation set that supports the claim, at least once, in front of both PM and PMM, before certification. It is a ten-minute ritual and it prevents a class of failure that otherwise takes two quarters to surface.

4.6 What mature companies actually do, as opposed to what they say

Large firms describe their handoff as governed by a launch review board applying documented criteria. Observation of how those boards actually function suggests something different and more interesting: the board is usually a capacity-allocation committee wearing the costume of a quality gate. Its real output is a ranked list of which launches get scarce product marketing attention, and its criteria are ostensibly about market impact but in practice weight the seniority of the requesting executive heavily. This is not necessarily corrupt; executive sponsorship is a genuine signal about strategic priority and is cheaper to observe than a forecast. But it means that a PM who prepares for the board by perfecting their impact estimate and neglecting their sponsorship is optimising the wrong variable, and a PM who understands the board's real function will spend their preparation differently. The second thing mature companies do that they rarely document is maintain an informal pre-clearance channel: the PM and PMM agree the claim privately weeks before the board, so the board ratifies rather than decides. The boards that work are the ones where this shadow process is acknowledged and shortened into the formal one; the ones that do not work are where the formal process is defended and the shadow process runs anyway, doubling the elapsed time.

5 Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: the expert asks who signs, not who was informed. The competent practitioner builds a responsibility matrix and feels covered. The expert reads the same matrix and asks a different question: for each market-facing claim, which single named person's judgement is on the line if it turns out false? The tell-tale sign in the wild is the blank pause. Ask a launch team "who signs the accuracy number" and a healthy team names someone in under three seconds; an unhealthy one produces a discussion about the process by which the number was agreed. The obvious reading — that this is a blame-allocation exercise — is wrong and is why the question is resisted. Its actual function is informational: a claim with a signatory gets checked, because the signatory checks it, and a claim owned by a process gets checked by nobody.

Two: positioning failure appears first in pipeline mix, not in win rate. The competent practitioner monitors win rate and concludes that positioning is fine when it holds steady. The expert watches the composition of the pipeline, because mis-set positioning does not primarily lose deals you should have won; it creates deals you should never have had. The tell is a quarter in which opportunity count rises, average deal size falls, win rate is flat, and sales-cycle length creeps up — a pattern that reads as growth and is in fact the intake of a worse-fitting cohort. The cost lands two to four quarters later as churn, and by then the positioning change that caused it is too far in the past to be a candidate explanation. The obvious reading, that more pipeline is good, is wrong in a specific way: a wrongly-framed product attracts buyers who are solving an adjacent problem, and those buyers convert at a normal rate because the rep is persuasive, then fail to renew at an abnormal one.

Three: "involve product marketing earlier" is a capacity instruction disguised as an etiquette instruction. The competent practitioner hears the complaint about late loop-in and resolves to send the brief sooner. The expert asks what product marketing will stop doing. The tell is a product marketing lead who says yes to every request and is late on most of them, combined with a launch calendar where the number of top-tier launches has grown every year. Sending the brief earlier into a saturated queue produces an earlier acknowledgement and the same delivery date. The obvious reading — that lateness reflects poor prioritisation by the PMM — is usually wrong; lateness at high utilisation is a property of the system, not of the person, and the only real interventions are adding capacity, reducing admissions, or shortening the service time per launch through templating.

Four: names are the most expensive irreversible artefact and are usually decided by accident. The competent practitioner treats naming as a copy task near the end. The expert treats it as a category claim made early, because a name tells a buyer what shelf the product sits on, and shelves determine budget lines, procurement categories and comparison sets. The tell is that the feature's name first appears in an engineering ticket, and the second tell is that nobody can say what the name is asserting. Kolam Verify is a good name precisely because "verify" places the product in the assurance category rather than the extraction category, which is worth several percentage points of price; had it shipped as "Kolam Auto-Extract Pro", the same software would have been compared against document-extraction tools priced a third lower. The obvious reading — that naming is subjective and therefore unimportant — confuses the absence of a right answer with the absence of consequences.

Five: product marketing's most valuable act is the refusal. The competent practitioner evaluates a PMM by the quality of the assets produced. The expert evaluates by the quality of what was declined: the launch downgraded, the claim softened, the number removed from the deck, the press briefing postponed. The tell is a product marketing function that has never in memory said no to a launch tier or struck a claim; such a function is an execution service and will not protect the company from an overclaim. The obvious reading is that a co-operative PMM is a good partner. In fact a PMM who never refuses has been trained by the organisation to believe refusal is not available to them, and the cost of that training arrives as a claim nobody was willing to challenge.

Six: most enablement value sits in support and customer success, not sales. The competent practitioner builds a launch plan weighted towards sales assets, because sales is loud and revenue is proximate. The expert notices that after launch, the volume of conversations about the product is dominated by support and success, that those conversations are with existing customers whose renewal is more valuable than a new logo, and that a support agent repeating a wrong explanation does so hundreds of times. The tell is a launch plan with six sales artefacts and one support macro. The cost of getting this wrong is not a lost deal; it is a slow accumulation of customers with a subtly wrong mental model of the product, which surfaces as feature-request noise that misleads the roadmap.

Seven: win-loss analysis is usually win-confirmation. The competent practitioner runs win-loss interviews and reports the themes. The expert interrogates the sampling. The tells are specific and easy to check: are lost deals interviewed at the same rate as won ones; is the rep present on the call; how long after the decision does the interview happen; and are no-decision outcomes — usually the largest category in enterprise — sampled at all. A programme that interviews wins promptly and losses eventually, with the rep listening, produces a systematically flattering picture that then shapes the next positioning cycle. The obvious reading — that win-loss data is objective market feedback — ignores that it is an instrument with a measurable bias, and an instrument whose bias is unknown is worse than no instrument because it carries false authority.

Eight: deprecation has no handoff, and does the most brand damage per rupee. The competent practitioner runs a disciplined process for launching things and no process at all for withdrawing them. The expert knows that a sunset is a claim reversal — the company is unsaying something it previously said — and that the affected population is, by definition, the subset of customers who adopted what the company asked them to adopt. The tell is a deprecation notice sent from an engineering alias, with a date and no alternative, that product marketing first sees when a customer forwards it. The cost of catching this late is disproportionate because the damage is concentrated in the most loyal cohort and because it teaches the field that the company's announcements cannot be relied on, which raises the price of every future claim.

Nine: the PM's persona and the PMM's segment are different objects with the same name. The competent practitioner notices that both functions talk about "the customer" and assumes they mean the same thing. They usually do not. A PM's persona is a behavioural construct built for design decisions — what this person is trying to do, in what context, with what constraints. A PMM's segment is a commercial construct built for targeting — a firmographic or demographic slice with a budget, a buying process and a media reachability. The tell is a meeting in which both parties agree enthusiastically and then produce artefacts that do not fit each other: a product designed for the operations manager and a campaign aimed at the CFO. The reconciliation is not to merge the two constructs, which destroys both, but to write down the mapping explicitly: which segments contain which personas, and who in each segment signs the purchase order.

Ten: pricing is the archetypal orphaned decision. The competent practitioner knows that pricing is nominally product marketing's. The expert knows that in most companies pricing is a decision both functions believe the other owns, arrived at by triangulating a competitor's public page under time pressure the week before launch. The tell is the speed of the decision relative to its consequence: a number that will govern every deal for two years, settled in forty minutes. The obvious reading — that pricing is hard because willingness-to-pay data is scarce — is half right; the deeper reason is that pricing sits exactly on the knowledge seam, requiring cost-to-serve and usage data from product and competitive and buying-process data from marketing, and orphaned decisions are precisely the ones that need both halves. The diagnostic that works is to ask each function, separately, to name the three inputs the price was based on, and to compare the answers.

6 How the picture changes by product type and by stage

Much of what is written about this topic asserts differences across product types that do not survive contact with practice, so it is worth separating the real differences from the decorative ones. The underlying mechanics — claims have owners, decay and reversal costs; fidelity decays through relays; product marketing is a capacity-constrained queue — do not vary at all. What varies is which of the three binds first.

In consumer products the binding constraint is relay count, and it is one. The store listing, the first-run screen and the push notification are the entire chain, which means fidelity is near-perfect and measurement is near-total, and the handoff collapses into a shared experimentation backlog rather than a document transfer. The distinctive risk is the opposite of the enterprise one: because claims are so cheap to change, teams change them constantly and accumulate no positional memory, ending a year with better copy and no clearer idea of who the product is for. The competent consumer PM runs tests; the expert one keeps a written record of which positioning hypotheses have been tried and killed, because that record is the only durable asset the experimentation produces.

In business and enterprise products the binding constraint is fidelity, because the chain is long and the buyer is not the user. Everything about the enterprise handoff — certification, battlecards, the obsession with a single sentence — is an attempt to hold rn up. The distinctive risk is that the artefacts proliferate to the point where reps cannot find the right one, at which point fidelity falls for reasons that look like laziness and are actually a search problem. The enterprise-specific expert move is asset pruning: a good product marketing team retires more collateral each quarter than it creates.

In platform and marketplace businesses the binding constraint is sequencing between two audiences with divergent interests, as Khoj Bazaar found, and the handoff must specify order and framing, not just content. There is also a structural oddity worth naming: the platform's developers or sellers are simultaneously customers and part of the product, so a claim made to them is also a claim about them, and the claim ledger needs entries for both directions.

In hardware and physical goods the binding constraint is substrate reversibility, as set out above, plus the channel's role as an uncontrolled relay. The genuine difference here is that a portion of the handoff is irrevocably complete months before the product is finished, which no amount of process agility changes.

In AI-native products the binding constraint is claim decay, and it is the newest and least well-handled of the four. It is also the one where the competent and the expert diverge most sharply today, simply because the practice is young: a great many launches in this category currently ship with an undated benchmark number and no re-certification owner, which is the same mistake Kolam made and will look, in five years, as obviously wrong as shipping without an escalation path looks now.

Stage changes the handoff in one substantive way and several cosmetic ones. The cosmetic ones are well known: early companies have no product marketing function and the PM does both jobs; large companies have too much process. The substantive one is the shape of the risk. In a company of thirty people the risk is that nobody notices positioning is a decision at all, and the company builds a good product with no shelf to sit on. Between roughly fifty and three hundred people — the stage where both protagonists sit — the risk changes character: a product marketing function now exists, but it is small, its authority is unsettled, and the number of launches has grown faster than the team, so the failure is queue saturation misread as laziness. Above a thousand people the risk inverts again, to the portfolio and arbitration problems of section 4.1, where the binding scarcity is not product marketing hours but a coherent story across products. A PM who carries the wrong stage's mental model into a company is reliably wrong: the ex-large-company PM arrives at a hundred-person firm and installs a launch council nobody has capacity to staff, and the ex-startup PM arrives at a large one and negotiates the boundary afresh with every launch, consuming exactly the transaction costs the standing framework exists to avoid.

7 Three worked cases, including one that failed

7.1 Kolam Labs: the claim with no date

Return to the 3 November thread. Sandhya and Meera had nineteen days, two signed pilots with an accuracy clause, a certified sales force and a benchmark that now returned three different numbers depending on the file mix. They considered three options and priced them roughly.

Option one was to hold the claim and launch as planned, on the argument that the internal benchmark had improved and the pilot-specific degradation was an artefact of two customers' unusual documents. Expected cost: if either pilot measured its own rate, the discovery would occur inside the contractual review window, with a renegotiation Meera estimated at a quarter's delay on roughly ₹1.2 crore of committed revenue plus the reputational cost with a risk committee. She put the probability of detection within ninety days at 0.7, giving an expected cost well over ₹80 lakh.

Option two was to delay the launch by four weeks to re-tune and re-benchmark. Direct cost was modest, but the launch sat inside a window when two lenders were making annual platform decisions, and missing it cost an estimated ₹70–90 lakh of pipeline with a high probability of about 0.6.

Option three, which they took, was to relaunch the claim rather than the product: replace a single global accuracy number with a scoped one — "clears 94 per cent of standard retail files on the September benchmark; we will measure your mix in the first two weeks and commit to a number for your portfolio" — and convert the pilot clause from a fixed threshold to a measured baseline with an improvement commitment. This is a weaker claim and a better product promise, and it required re-certifying forty-one reps in eleven days on a sentence most of them liked less than the old one. The re-certification used Meera's write-it-from-memory test; the first pass returned three of six acceptable, the sentence was cut from thirty-one words to nineteen, and the second pass returned five of six.

The durable change was structural rather than verbal. Kolam added model releases to the launch calendar as first-class events, gave every externally-stated performance number a version tag and an owner, and instituted the seven-day re-check rule. Six months later the measurable effect was not on win rate, which moved within noise, but on a metric nobody had been tracking: the number of customer escalations categorised as "product did not do what we were told" fell from nine in the preceding half-year to two.

7.2 Kanthi Diagnostics: moving the claim to a cheaper substrate

Arvind and Priyanka's resolution has already been described in outline; the numbers are worth completing because they show the trade being made. Printing the fourteen-minute claim on the carton on 6 October carried an expected cost of ₹25.9 lakh by the ledger. Moving it to the quick-start card, printed in January on a nineteen-day lead, reduced C from ₹74 lakh to about ₹9 lakh because the reprint was small and the channel catalogue was untouched, and it also reduced p from 0.35 to about 0.12 because by January the firmware had thirty days of field data from twenty instruments. Expected cost fell from ₹25.9 lakh to roughly ₹1.1 lakh. The cost of the move was softer carton copy — "faster daily quality control" instead of a number — which Priyanka estimated, from two partner conversations, might reduce catalogue-driven enquiries by a tenth.

The second-order effect was the one that surprised both of them. Because the precise claim now lived on a January artefact, product marketing had a legitimate reason to be in the December firmware review, which it had never previously attended. The measurement discipline that followed — twenty instruments, three lots, thirty days, median and not mean — came out of that meeting, and the number that emerged was not fourteen minutes but eleven and a half. Had the carton been printed in October, Kanthi would have spent the year defending a number its own data did not support. It shipped eleven and a half and sold it comfortably, because the comparison that mattered to a lab manager was against eighteen, not against a competitor's brochure.

7.3 Kalanidhi Learning: the failure, and what recovery actually looked like

Kalanidhi Learning sold a subscription app for spoken-English fluency, priced at ₹399 a month, with about 180,000 monthly actives concentrated in tier-two cities and a customer-acquisition motion that was almost entirely paid social plus app-store search. In the March quarter of 2026 its new head of growth and its product marketing lead agreed a repositioning: away from "practice spoken English with an AI partner", which tested as vague, towards "clear your job interview in ninety days", which tested dramatically better on every creative metric they had. 8 Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of late detection

The failures below are ordered by how long they take to become visible, which is roughly the inverse of how much attention they get.

The unowned claim. Early warning: a performance number appears in more than two documents with no version, date or named owner. Diagnostic question: who would we call if this number were wrong on Monday? Cost of late detection: proportional to repetitions before correction, which is why it compounds; Kolam's exposure at nineteen days was a contract renegotiation, and at nineteen weeks it would have been a renewal cycle.

Queue saturation misread as indiscipline. Early warning: product marketing accepts every request and misses most dates, while the proportion of top-tier launches rises year on year. Diagnostic question: what did we decline last quarter, and who declined it? Cost of late detection: the organisation concludes it has a people problem, replaces the product marketing lead, and reproduces the same queue with a new name on it.

The positioning U-turn after the funnel is built. Early warning: a repositioning is approved on creative-test data alone, with no product-side sign-off and no claim about what the product will now have to do. Diagnostic question: what would have to be true of the product for this claim to hold, and is it true today? Cost of late detection: Kalanidhi's three quarters, and a cohort of refund-seeking customers who leave public ratings.

The orphaned pricing decision. Early warning: nobody can produce the working file behind the price. Diagnostic question: name the three inputs, and who supplied each. Cost of late detection: a price that sales discounts away in every deal, which is expensive not because of the discount but because the discount teaches the market the list price is fictional, and re-establishing a credible list price takes a full renewal cycle.

Enablement theatre. Early warning: a certification with a hundred per cent pass rate. Diagnostic question: pull six reps at random and have them write the claim from memory. Cost of late detection: a quarter of pipeline built on four incompatible descriptions of the product, and a support queue that inherits the confusion for two quarters after that.

Benchmark rot. Early warning: the evaluation set behind a public number was last refreshed more than two model generations ago, or was assembled by whoever was free. Diagnostic question: who owns the evaluation set, and when was it last changed? Cost of late detection: the claim and the product diverge silently, and the divergence is discovered by a customer with a sample the company never tested.

Silent deprecation. Early warning: a sunset date exists in an engineering plan and in no marketing plan. Diagnostic question: who is writing the note, and what are we offering instead? Cost of late detection: concentrated damage among the customers who did exactly what the company asked.

Portfolio contradiction. Early warning: two products' collateral answer the same buyer question differently and neither team has read the other's. Diagnostic question: if a customer bought both, what would they think we think the difference is? Cost of late detection: the contradiction is discovered in a competitive deal, by the competitor.

Almost every diagnostic in this section is a question about a person, not a document. That is not stylistic. A document can be produced without anyone having thought; a name cannot be produced without someone having accepted consequences.

9 Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements in this field are real, held by serious practitioners, and unresolved by evidence. They are presented here in their strongest form, with what each rests on and what would have to be true for it to be wrong. A reader who wants a synthesis will be disappointed; none of these has one that anybody actually holds.

9.1 Should product marketing be able to stop a launch?

The case for the gate. Claims impose liabilities on the whole firm, and liabilities require a party with standing to refuse. The strongest evidence comes from regulated industries, where mandatory claim clearance demonstrably reduces the incidence of retractions, and from the observation — supported by the ledger arithmetic above — that the expected cost of a bad claim on an irreversible substrate routinely exceeds the cost of a four-week delay by an order of magnitude. On this view a launch gate is no more controversial than a security review, and the objection that it slows teams down is an objection to the existence of risk management.

The case against. Gates do not improve judgement; they relocate it to people with less context and more distance, and they reliably degrade into ceremony. The empowered-team evidence is that accountability must be single-threaded to be real, and that a gate lets the accountable team believe the gate is the safeguard, which reduces the care they take. There is also a measurable second-order effect: gates increase batch size, because teams bundle changes to amortise the review, and larger batches are riskier than the risk the gate was created to manage.

What would settle it. The pro-gate position would be wrong if most claim failures turned out to originate in the reviewing function's own blind spots rather than the team's, or if gated organisations showed higher, not lower, retraction rates once launch volume is controlled for. The anti-gate position would be wrong if the cost of retractions in ungated organisations scaled with launch volume in a way that no amount of team accountability suppressed. Nobody has published data good enough to decide this, and the honest practitioner position is conditional: gate the irreversible and the externally-regulated, do not gate the rest.

9.2 Upstream partner or downstream commercialiser?

The upstream case. Positioning decisions change what should be built, so a product marketer who arrives after the spec is frozen can only describe a decision that has already foreclosed most of the interesting options. The evidence is the repositioning literature and a long tail of cases in which the same software, re-aimed, sold at several times the price — which demonstrates that market frame and engineering content are separable, and that the frame is often the higher-leverage of the two.

The downstream case. Real firms have one product marketer for every four to eight product managers. Upstream involvement in everything is not a philosophy, it is a staffing fantasy, and pretending otherwise produces a function spread so thin that it is upstream nowhere and reliable nowhere. Better, on this view, to define a crisp interface, be excellent at commercialisation, and reserve upstream involvement for the two or three bets a year where the category is genuinely in question. The evidence is the queueing arithmetic of Figure 2 and the repeated observation that firms which mandate early involvement without funding it simply add a meeting.

What would settle it. The upstream case is wrong if the value of early involvement is concentrated in a small minority of launches, in which case selective engagement dominates. The downstream case is wrong if the launches that turn out to matter cannot be identified in advance — and there is decent reason to think they cannot, since the products that create categories frequently look minor at brief-writing time. This is the sharpest live disagreement in the field, and a practitioner's position on it is usually a function of whether their firm's biggest recent win came from a bet nobody flagged early.

9.3 Dedicated or pooled product marketing?

Dedicated. Depth wins. A product marketer embedded with one product team learns the specific knowledge that briefs cannot transfer, catches the accuracy problem, and earns the standing to refuse. Pooled. Depth is expensive and duplicative; a pooled team sees the whole portfolio, prevents contradiction, and can be allocated against the queue rather than stranded on a quiet product. The pooled model wins the portfolio-coherence argument, as section 4.1 suggests; the dedicated model wins the claim-accuracy argument. Both are right about what they measure, which is why large firms oscillate between them on roughly a three-year cycle, and why the oscillation itself is more costly than either steady state.

9.4 Does positioning matter in product-led and AI-native businesses?

The sceptical case, steelmanned. In a self-serve business with a strong first-run experience, distribution and activation dominate outcomes by a wide margin; the positioning statement is a post-hoc rationalisation of whatever the product's best-performing surface happens to say. Teams that obsess over category selection while their activation rate sits at eleven per cent are optimising the smaller term. In AI-native products, the argument goes further: capability moves so fast that any category the firm picks will be obsolete within a year, and committing to one is a liability.

The reply. Category selection determines what buyers search for, which budget line funds the purchase, and which comparison set the buyer assembles — all of which precede the first-run experience and determine who ever reaches it. The observable test is whether the firm's best accounts arrived through a search intent it chose or one it inherited. On the AI-specific point, the reply is that fast-moving capability raises the value of a durable category claim rather than lowering it, because the category is the one thing a buyer can hold on to when the underlying capability changes monthly. Neither side has conceded, and the empirical work that would separate them — controlled variation in category framing with downstream cohort tracking — is rarely run because it is expensive and slow.

10 What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic can describe the handoff, name the artefacts, and run a competent launch. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in ways that are visible within about a week of watching them work.

They start from the claim rather than the calendar. Given a launch, their first question is not "when do we brief marketing" but "what are we going to tell people, and what would make it false", and the artefacts fall out of that rather than out of a template. They speak about reversibility unprompted, and they can tell you which decisions on their current launch are irreversible and why, which most practitioners cannot. They carry a working estimate of their product marketing partner's capacity and treat it as a real constraint rather than a personality trait, which means they arrive with a proposal about what to drop rather than a request to add. They keep the number of things they say to three, because they know the fourth will be the one repeated wrongly.

They are comfortable making the claim weaker. This is the single behaviour that most separates the two populations, because weakening a claim costs something immediate and visible — a duller headline, a softer carton, a less impressive number — and saves something distant and invisible, and the person who does it must be willing to be the least exciting voice in the room. They ask the write-it-from-memory question rather than the did-you-understand question. They read pipeline composition before pipeline volume. They treat a product marketer's refusal as evidence the function is working rather than as an obstruction. They notice when a decision has become an orphan, and they pick it up rather than escalating it, on the reasoning that an orphaned decision made adequately by whoever is present beats a perfect one made too late by the right person. And when a claim does turn out to be false, they correct it quickly, in public, and at the same volume at which it was made, because they understand that the durable asset in this discipline is not any individual claim but the market's willingness to believe the next one.

11 What each protagonist decided

Sandhya Balakrishnan launched Kolam Verify on 22 November 2026, three days later than planned, with a scoped and dated accuracy claim, a re-certified sales force of forty-one, two pilot contracts rewritten from fixed thresholds to measured baselines, and a new standing rule that no production model change could reach an accuracy-committed account without a seven-day claim re-check signed by her and by Meera Kuruvilla jointly. Her reasoning, offered to a sceptical revenue leader who preferred the bigger number, was narrowly commercial rather than ethical: the old claim's expected cost of error exceeded the revenue at stake in the launch window, and no forecast that ignored that cost was a forecast. She also conceded something in the same conversation that is worth noting, because it is the part most PMs omit — that the weaker claim probably did cost Kolam two deals that quarter, and that she could not prove it had saved more than it cost. She made the decision anyway, on the grounds that the distribution of outcomes mattered more than its mean.

Arvind Ramanathan let the carton go to press on 6 October carrying two durable claims and no number, moved the fourteen-minute claim to the January quick-start card and the channel deck, and attended the December firmware review at Priyanka Deshmukh's insistence. The measured figure came back at eleven and a half minutes, which he shipped. The Kanthi K2 launched on 12 February 2027 into the financial-year-end buying season with a claim its own field data supported and a channel that had been trained on the softer carton copy six weeks earlier. Arvind's private view, expressed later to a colleague, was that the decision had been made for him by arithmetic he should have done a year earlier on a different product, and that the discipline he actually acquired was not the ledger but the habit of asking, of every sentence that would reach a customer, what its substrate was and who would have to take it back.

Discussion questions

1. Kolam and Kanthi both chose a weaker claim over a stronger one. In each case the cost of the weaker claim was immediate and estimable, and the benefit was probabilistic and unprovable. Under what circumstances is a product manager right to accept that trade — and how should a firm compensate a manager whose good decisions are, by construction, invisible in the outcome data?

2. Kalanidhi's repositioning improved every metric owned by growth and degraded every metric owned by product, and was reported as a success for a full quarter. Is this primarily a measurement failure, an organisational-design failure, or a failure of the product manager who had reservations and did not press them? What specific mechanism would have caught it in April rather than in July, and what would that mechanism have cost in the cases where the repositioning was in fact correct?

3. Section 9.1 leaves the gate question unresolved. Take a position: should product marketing at a firm of your choosing hold the right to stop a launch? Specify which launches, on what criteria, who hears the appeal — and what evidence you would collect over the next four quarters that would make you reverse your answer.

12 Going deeper

Launch planning and launch mistakes — the operational container this topic sits inside; it matters next because the claim ledger and the tiering queue both have to be scheduled against a real launch calendar, and it unlocks the ability to see which launch mistakes are planning errors and which are decision-rights errors wearing a planning costume.

Dividing PM and PMM responsibilities — the direct continuation, moving from the handoff event to the standing boundary; it matters because most of the artefacts in Figure 1 recur every quarter and deserve a standing rule rather than a negotiation, and it unlocks the org-design conversation about dedicated versus pooled structures left open in section 9.3.

What a GTM strategy is — the level above this one, where segment, channel, pricing and motion are chosen together; it matters because a handoff can only be as coherent as the strategy it serves, and it unlocks the question of why a firm has the channel structure that sets Kanthi's relay problem in the first place.

Your first 100 users — the early-stage counterpart, where there is no product marketing function and the founder holds every claim; it matters because the habits formed at that stage determine whether claims are ever treated as objects, and it unlocks a sharper view of when a firm actually needs its first product marketing hire.

Channels: paid, owned, earned — the distribution surfaces on which claims travel; it matters because each channel has a different relay coefficient and a different reversal cost, which is the machinery of Figure 1 applied to media, and it unlocks a more precise view of where a claim will be repeated and how often.

Inbound versus outbound — the demand-creation split that determines whether the buyer arrives with a frame already formed; it matters because inbound buyers self-select into a category the firm may not have chosen, and it unlocks the search-intent argument that the sceptics in section 9.4 have to answer.

Product-led growth — the single-relay world, where the product is the claim and experimentation replaces enablement; it matters because it is the limiting case that tests every argument on this page, and it unlocks the question of what product marketing is for when there are no salespeople to enable.

Sales-led growth — the many-relay world, where fidelity is the binding constraint and enablement is the central craft; it matters because the arithmetic of Table 3 becomes the dominant consideration, and it unlocks the revenue-enablement school's strongest ground.
