Working with Product Marketing

What product marketing owns, and what a product manager hands over

On the second Monday of January 2027, Ananya Rao pulled up the launch calendar for Dwipa Systems and did the arithmetic she should have done six weeks earlier. Dwipa Compliance Shield — the statutory-filing automation module she had spent four months building with a team of nine engineers — was scheduled to go live on 24 February, thirty-nine days away. Dwipa sold HR and payroll software to mid-market Indian manufacturers and logistics firms, roughly four hundred customers paying an average of ₹38 lakh a year, and Compliance Shield was meant to close the single most common objection her sales team heard from prospects: that statutory returns under the new labour codes were still being filed by hand in a spreadsheet bolted onto the product. Ananya had a working feature, a demo that impressed her VP of Engineering, and — she now realised, looking at the calendar — no launch narrative, no pricing decision, no sales deck, and no one outside her own team who had ever heard the phrase "Compliance Shield" before that morning's staff meeting.

This was not her first launch. Eleven months earlier Dwipa had shipped a leave-management redesign that, by every engineering measure, worked perfectly and, by every commercial measure, underperformed for two full quarters. Support tickets asked what the feature even was. Sales reps described it in four different, mutually inconsistent ways on four different calls the same week, because nobody had told them what to say. The head of product marketing, Rohit Sabharwal, had been looped in nine days before that launch, largely to "help publicise" something he had had no hand in shaping — and he had said, more than once since, that nine days was not a heads-up, it was an ambush. Ananya did not want to repeat that mistake, and the honest reason she nearly did again was that she had never been taught, precisely, where her job ended and Rohit's began. That is the gap this page exists to close.

1 The idea: a division of labour, not a courtesy CC

Product marketing is the function responsible for translating what a product does into why a specific buyer should care, and for equipping every customer-facing team — sales, support, partnerships, the website itself — to say that consistently. Where a product manager's accountability runs from customer problem to shipped solution, a product marketing manager's accountability runs from shipped solution to market outcome: positioning, pricing and packaging, messaging, sales enablement, launch tiering, and analyst or press relations where those exist. The handoff is not a single meeting or a single document. It is the explicit, scheduled transfer of specific decisions and specific artifacts from the PM's desk to the PMM's desk, early enough that the PMM's work can shape the product's final shape rather than merely narrate it after the fact.

The distinction has an intellectual history worth knowing, because it explains why so many companies get it wrong. Regis McKenna argued in the 1980s that in mature technology markets the product is inseparable from how it is positioned in the customer's mind — marketing was not decoration applied after engineering finished, it was a design input. Geoffrey Moore formalised this in Crossing the Chasm (1991) with a rigorous positioning template — target customer, need, category, key benefit, primary competitive alternative, key differentiator — that remains the backbone of most product marketing training programmes today. The modern SaaS-era articulation, and the one most directly useful to a working PM, comes from April Dunford's 2019 book Obviously Awesome: positioning is not a tagline, it is a set of decisions about which market you are competing in and which attributes matter in that market, and those decisions have to be made before messaging is written, not after. Product marketing as a distinct, PM-adjacent discipline — separate from brand marketing and separate from demand generation — crystallised through the 2000s and 2010s as software shifted to product-led and sales-assisted models that needed someone dedicated to the translation layer between roadmap and revenue.

The sentence Ananya could say in a leadership meeting without sounding glib is this one, and it is worth memorising exactly:

"I own the problem and the solution; product marketing owns whether the market understands and wants the solution I built — and the handoff is the point at which those two jobs have to agree on the same story."

2 How the handoff actually works, mechanically

The mechanics fall into four steps that practitioners at well-run companies treat as fixed, but that most first-time PMs never see written down anywhere, which is exactly why Ananya had never seen them. The first step is early exposure, not a finished brief: the PMM needs to see the customer problem and the roughly-shaped solution while it is still malleable — typically eight to ten weeks before a meaningful launch — because positioning decisions (which competitor you are implicitly compared against, which customer segment you are speaking to first) can still change what gets built, not just how it is described. Bringing PMM in after the spec is frozen turns a strategic partner into a copywriter.

The second step is a joint launch-tiering decision: PM and PMM together classify how much market noise the release deserves, because the amount of PMM investment — sales certification, analyst briefing, press outreach, in-app announcement, a release-notes line and nothing else — should be proportional to expected impact, not to how proud engineering is of the work. The third step is artifact ownership, an explicit list of who drafts what, who approves what, and who is merely informed — this is where most ambiguity festers, and it is solved with a written RACI, not a verbal understanding that erodes under deadline pressure. The fourth step is the enablement and feedback loop: PMM trains sales and support before launch day, and after launch, win-loss data and support ticket themes flow back to the PM as input to the next roadmap cycle, closing what would otherwise be a one-way handoff into a genuine loop.

3 A worked example: scoring the launch tier, twice

Rohit's team at Dwipa used a simple scoring model, adapted from the RICE framework popular among SaaS product marketing teams, to decide how much investment a launch deserved before a single word of messaging was written: Launch Score = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort, where Reach is the number of accounts affected in the next two quarters, Impact is a 1–3 scale of revenue or retention consequence, Confidence is a percentage reflecting how sure the team is of that impact estimate, and Effort is person-weeks of PMM time required. For Compliance Shield, Ananya and Rohit sat down in the second week of January and worked the numbers together.

Reach: 210 of Dwipa's roughly 400 customers operated in states where the new labour-code filing requirement applied, so Reach = 210. Impact: statutory non-compliance carried real penalty risk for customers, and three enterprise accounts worth ₹1.4 crore combined had named this exact gap in their renewal conversations, so the team scored Impact at 3, the top of the scale. Confidence: the engineering build was complete and tested against two pilot customers, so Confidence = 80%, expressed as 0.8. Effort: a full launch tier — sales certification, a compliance-specific one-pager, an analyst briefing with a labour-law commentator, and a customer webinar — was estimated at 6 person-weeks of Rohit's team's time.

Score = (210 × 3 × 0.8) ÷ 6 = 504 ÷ 6 = 84. Against Dwipa's internal thresholds (Tier 1 above 60, Tier 2 between 25 and 60, Tier 3 below 25), 84 put Compliance Shield comfortably in Tier 1: full enablement, an analyst briefing, and a customer webinar, all funded and staffed.

Now the second pass, showing how one changed input moves the whole decision. Three days later, Dwipa's legal counsel flagged that the interpretation of the new filing rule in two of the pilot states was still under central-government clarification, which meant the feature might need a mid-quarter correction. Confidence dropped from 0.8 to 0.4. Recomputing: Score = (210 × 3 × 0.4) ÷ 6 = 252 ÷ 6 = 42 — still respectable, but now squarely Tier 2. Rohit's team scaled back accordingly: sales enablement and the one-pager stayed, but the analyst briefing was postponed until the regulatory language settled, and the customer webinar was replaced with a lighter email sequence. Nothing about the engineering work changed; the market-facing investment changed because the confidence in the claim they could responsibly make had changed. This is the calculation a launch tier actually is — not a gut feeling about how excited the team is.

4 Nuances a learner must become aware of

Positioning is not messaging

Positioning is the strategic decision about which market you compete in, which segment you speak to first, and which two or three attributes matter most in that segment; messaging is the words used to communicate a positioning that has already been decided. Most first-time PMs skip straight to messaging — asking PMM to "write some copy" — without ever settling the prior question of which competitive frame the product should be judged against. Compliance Shield could be positioned against manual spreadsheet processes (a category-creation play, competing against the status quo) or against dedicated compliance point solutions like a standalone labour-law filing tool (a head-to-head play). Those two choices produce entirely different messaging, pricing, and even feature-priority decisions, and they cannot both be true at once.

The handoff has a direction, but it is not one-way

It is tempting to treat the handoff as PM finishing a relay leg and passing a baton that PMM then runs with alone. In a healthy loop, PMM's market research — competitor teardown, analyst conversation, win-loss interview — flows back into the PM's next roadmap cycle. Companies that treat the handoff as strictly one-directional end up with a PMM function that repeats stale positioning launch after launch, because nobody is feeding it fresh input.

"PMM was informed" is not the same as "PMM was consulted"

Being copied on a Slack channel or invited to a launch review two weeks out satisfies almost no one's actual definition of partnership, yet PMs routinely believe it does because a name appears somewhere in the thread. The RACI in Table 1 exists precisely to make this distinction impossible to fudge: an "I" is not a "C", and neither is an "A/R".

Launch tiering is a resourcing tool, not a status symbol

Engineers and PMs alike tend to want every release treated as Tier 1, because a smaller tier can feel like a verdict on the work's importance. It is not; it is a statement about expected market impact relative to available PMM capacity, and treating every release as Tier 1 exhausts a PMM team's finite hours on low-impact work, leaving genuinely important launches under-resourced when they arrive.

Pricing and packaging decisions belong to PMM, but the inputs belong to PM

Because PMM typically holds the pen on final price points and packaging tiers, PMs sometimes assume they have no say. In practice, PM owns the cost-to-serve data, the usage patterns that reveal willingness to pay, and the competitive feature comparison — the raw inputs a defensible pricing decision requires. A PM who disengages from pricing entirely, on the theory that "that's PMM's job," is withholding exactly the information PMM needs to do that job well.

What the handoff cannot tell you

No amount of disciplined handoff process will rescue a product that solves a problem customers do not actually have, or compensate for a sales team that is structurally incentivised to sell the wrong segment. The handoff improves the odds that a good product is understood and sold correctly; it does not evaluate whether the product was worth building in the first place, and treating a clean handoff as proof of product-market fit is a category error.

Confusion with "marketing" broadly, and with demand generation specifically

PMM is frequently conflated with brand marketing (which builds the company's overall reputation) or demand generation (which runs the campaigns that fill the sales pipeline). PMM sits between product and those two functions, supplying the positioning and proof points that brand and demand-gen teams then amplify. A PM who hands a feature to demand generation without going through PMM first usually produces technically accurate but strategically incoherent campaign copy.

The questions a thoughtful newcomer should ask before relying on this model

Before assuming a clean PM-PMM split will work at a given company, a newcomer should ask: does a dedicated PMM function even exist here, or is a generalist marketer covering five roles at once? Is there an agreed launch-tiering threshold, or is tiering decided by whoever argues loudest? And critically — does leadership actually enforce the eight-week lead time, or does "we'll loop in marketing later" quietly become the default under deadline pressure, as it nearly did for Ananya?

5 Consumer, B2B, and marketplace — and how stage changes it

In consumer products, PMM's centre of gravity is app-store copy, push notification strategy, and influencer or creator partnerships, because the buyer and the user are the same person making a fast, largely unassisted decision; the handoff artifact that matters most is the in-app announcement and the store listing, and it needs to be ready days, not weeks, before a release given how quickly consumer app rankings respond to messaging. In B2B products like Dwipa's, PMM's centre of gravity is the sales battlecard, the analyst relationship, and the case study, because the buyer is rarely the user and the sales cycle is long enough that enablement quality compounds across dozens of deals; a battlecard error propagates through every rep's pipeline for a full quarter. In marketplace products, PMM has to speak to two audiences with different, sometimes conflicting incentives — supply-side sellers and demand-side buyers — and the handoff has to specify explicitly which side's messaging ships first, because a change that delights buyers can simultaneously alarm sellers, and PMM needs the PM's supply-liquidity data to know how much room there is to push.

Stage changes the handoff's formality more than its substance. At an early-stage company with no dedicated PMM hire, the PM typically performs a compressed version of both roles personally, and the risk is skipping the positioning discipline entirely under the excuse that "we're too small for that." At a large company like Dwipa, with a PMM function of a dozen people organised by segment, the risk inverts: the handoff becomes so process-heavy — templates, sign-off chains, a launch review committee — that it takes longer to agree on a positioning statement than it took to build the feature, and the eight-week runway becomes a floor that keeps rising.

6 Common mistakes

The late loop-in. Symptom: PMM receives the first briefing document inside three weeks of launch and visibly scrambles. Underlying misunderstanding: treating PMM as an announcement service rather than a strategic partner in shaping the product's market frame. Cheapest diagnostic: check the calendar date on which PMM's name first appears in any launch document — if it is inside six weeks of ship date, the loop-in was late regardless of how the launch ultimately performs.

The unscoped tier. Symptom: every release gets a press-worthy launch plan regardless of actual customer reach. Underlying misunderstanding: conflating engineering effort or personal pride with market impact. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what the Reach and Impact numbers were, in writing, before the tier was assigned — if no one can produce them, the tier was assigned by feeling.

The silent pricing decision. Symptom: PMM announces a price point that sales immediately discounts away in every deal. Underlying misunderstanding: PMM set price without the cost-to-serve and willingness-to-pay data that only PM and sales operations hold. Cheapest diagnostic: ask PMM to name the three data points the price was based on — vague answers reveal a guess dressed as a decision.

The one-way handoff. Symptom: the same objections and the same competitive comparisons resurface, unaddressed, launch after launch. Underlying misunderstanding: treating the post-launch win-loss review as optional rather than as the mechanism that feeds market reality back into the next roadmap. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether the previous launch's win-loss findings appear anywhere in the current roadmap document — their absence means the loop never closed.

The cheapest diagnostic for almost every PM–PMM failure is the calendar: pull up when PMM's name first appears in the launch document, and you will usually already know how the launch went.

7 What good looks like

Six months after the leave-management stumble, Dwipa launched a smaller feature — bulk statutory-form uploads for HR administrators — the right way, and it is worth walking through as a contrast. Ananya brought Rohit into the problem definition in the same week she wrote the first product brief, nine weeks before the target ship date, before a single line of the specification was locked. Together they scored the launch at 34 — Reach of 140 customers, Impact of 2, Confidence of 0.9, Effort of 3 person-weeks — landing it cleanly in Tier 2: solid sales enablement and a release-notes feature, no press push. Rohit's team drafted the positioning against the explicit alternative of "administrators re-keying data from paper forms," not against a rival product, because that was the honestly larger competitive threat. Sales received a one-page battlecard eleven days before launch and ran a quiz on it in a Friday call; support received three macros and a two-line FAQ addition. Three weeks after launch, Rohit brought Ananya five verbatim quotes from customer calls, two of which described a workflow limitation Ananya folded directly into the next sprint. Nothing about this launch was dramatic. That, precisely, is what a handoff working correctly looks like: unremarkable, on schedule, and quietly closing the loop.

8 What Ananya decided, and what to learn next

Facing thirty-nine days and no positioning for Compliance Shield, Ananya did not try to compress nine weeks of handoff into five. She scoped it honestly: she and Rohit ran the tiering exercise that same week, landed on Tier 2 given the regulatory uncertainty, and agreed the launch would ship with a solid sales battlecard and a customer email sequence rather than the analyst briefing a Tier 1 launch would have earned. She also did something less obvious — she asked Rohit to build the post-launch win-loss review into the calendar before launch day arrived, not after, because the leave-management failure had taught her that the review that "gets scheduled later" tends never to happen at all. The reasoning she gave her VP was simple: a smaller, well-executed launch beats a large, half-supported one, and the eight-week runway she had missed this time was now a fixed line item on every future launch calendar she controlled.

The next idea worth studying, once this one is solid, is how PM and PMM divide responsibility for the messages that live inside the product itself — the in-app copy, onboarding flows, and empty states that neither function fully owns by default and that fall through the gap this page has just mapped. Two questions are worth sitting with before moving on: first, in your own organisation, is there a written threshold for launch tiers, or is tier assigned by whoever is most persuasive in the room that week? Second, if you pulled up the launch calendar for your last three releases right now, on what date would PMM's name first appear — and would you be comfortable if your VP asked you that question directly?

Two questions to sit with

1. Does your organisation have a written, numeric threshold for launch tiers — or is the tier decided by whoever argues loudest in the room?

2. If you checked your last three launch calendars today, how many days before ship date did product marketing's name first appear — and is that a number you would defend to your VP?

A teaching case on working with product marketing

1. Opening

On the morning of Friday, 9 October 2026, Bhavna Somani sat in the glass-walled meeting room on the second floor of Jhalak Dyehouse Systems' office in Bhilwara, Rajasthan,. As head of product, she had spent ten weeks building the Jhalak Shade Planner, a module that tells a dyeing house which machine, recipe and time slot to use so that a fabric lot matches the buyer's approved shade on the first attempt. The module was ready. The launch was fixed for Tuesday, 17 November, nine days after Diwali, when mills reopen and owners begin planning winter orders.

Six weeks earlier the company had hired its first product marketing manager, Indu Purohit, who worked from Bengaluru. Indu had been waiting for a handover that had not come. By the end of that day Bhavna had to tell her, and the whole company, exactly what product marketing would own for this launch and what product would keep.

2. Company background

Jhalak was founded in 2014 by a former production manager at a Bhilwara suiting mill. It began as a notebook-replacement for dye recipes, grew into a dyeing-house ERP covering lab dips, batch cards, machine loading and chemical stores, and now serves 212 processing sites across Bhilwara, Pali and Bhiwadi, with a growing handful around Surat. Annual recurring revenue is ₹22 crore and the company employs 96 people.

Its competitors are mostly indirect. Large integrated groups run SAP. Smaller mills keep accounts in Tally and Zoho Books and production in registers and WhatsApp groups. Global colour-management vendors such as Datacolor are priced for export houses, not a Pali job-work dyer. Jhalak's edge is that it speaks the shop floor's language, and its interface runs in Hindi as well as English.

The market is under pressure. Rajasthan's pollution-control norms for common effluent treatment plants punish waste, buyers demand tighter shade tolerances, and GST e-invoicing has already pushed even small mills towards software.

Bhavna Somani, head of product in Bhilwara, wants the launch to succeed and her roadmap to survive it.

Indu Purohit, product marketing manager in Bengaluru, joined on 1 September at ₹32 lakh a year. She wants clear ownership and access to customers. She has said plainly that she will not polish a story she did not shape.

Omprakash Rathore, sales head in Pali, wants something reps can say in a mill office in five minutes. He worries that a new role will slow him down before Diwali orders are closed.

5. The options

Option A: product keeps the launch. Bhavna retains positioning, messaging and pricing and asks Indu to handle channel content and sales training only. The upside is speed, since no handover is needed. The cost is 100 hours of her time, five weeks of roadmap delay, and a message that will still be built from a product brief rather than from the customer's words.

Option B: a structured handoff to product marketing. Bhavna gives Indu a written pack: the problem, the beta evidence, the target customer, what the product does not do and the price constraints. Product marketing owns the link between the product and the market: who the buyer is, what problem the buyer names in his own words, how the offer is positioned against alternatives, how it is packaged and priced, and how the sales team is equipped to carry it. Product owns the problem definition, the evidence, the roadmap and the truth of what the product can and cannot do. The launch is where the two meet, and the handover is the work of turning product's knowledge into a form marketing can act on.

A defensible path is Option B. The evidence for it is already in the exhibits. Exhibit 2 shows that the best message came from the field, not from the product brief, and that is precisely the information a PMM exists to find and spread. Exhibit 3 shows that 100 outstanding hours, most of them enablement and channel work, sit with the wrong owner. Exhibit 1 gives the raw material for a packaging discussion that Bhavna has neither the time nor the market view to do well.

The handoff should be specific. Bhavna passes on the beta data, the customer list and a short statement of limits, for example that the module does not yet handle blended fabrics. She also passes the pricing hypothesis, flagged as open. Indu owns the "fewer re-dyes" message, tests it in a Dhaka conversation with Uday and in the Dubai one-pager, makes a packaging recommendation to Bhavna and Omprakash by 16 October, and runs enablement from 26 October. Bhavna keeps veto on any claim the product cannot deliver. Any change to price for existing customers goes through Uday first.

The risk is real: Indu is new, and the launch date is close. Bhavna can reduce it by holding a two-hour role-play, with sales, engineering and finance in one room, to test the pack before it is final. If the pack cannot survive that session, the launch can slip one week without losing the post-Diwali window.

Sarvatra Ganna Systems: The Week the Message Changed

A case on the boundary between product and product marketing, set in the Uttar Pradesh cane belt, October 2026.

1. Gorakhpur, Sunday night

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Shubhangi Tripathi was still at her desk on the first floor of Sarvatra Ganna Systems' office on Park Road, Gorakhpur, with the fans off and the window open. On the screen in front of her were two documents that could not both be right.

The first was a forty-one-page handover pack, built over five weeks, that transferred the launch of Sarvatra Kanta Live from her product organisation to Ekta Chaubey, the company's first product marketing manager. It named the buyer, the problem, the evidence, the limits of the product and a pricing hypothesis, and it assigned positioning, messaging, packaging and enablement to Ekta. It was, Shubhangi thought, a good pack. Her previous employer would have shipped it.

The second was a WhatsApp export Ekta had sent at 9.40 that evening: forty-eight messages from the cane managers' group she had been added to in August, covering four weeks. In week one the managers had wanted to talk about payment speed. In week two, after a rumour that the State Advised Price would move, they wanted to talk about working capital. In week three, after two mills in Bahraich fell behind, they wanted to talk about what they could safely tell the Cane Commissioner's office. In week four they were back to payment speed, but only because a growers' society had started quoting Sarvatra's own website at a mill director in a public meeting.

Ekta's covering note had one line. "The pack positions a product. The market is asking a different question every Monday. Which of those am I supposed to own?"

By nine the next morning Shubhangi had to answer that question in front of Yogeshwar Pathak, the founder, because the Cane Commissioner's season notification was expected inside the fortnight and nobody in Gorakhpur controlled the date.

2. The company, and a signature from 2018

Sarvatra Ganna Systems was founded in Gorakhpur in 2017 by Yogeshwar Pathak, who had spent eleven years running the cane yard at a private mill in Deoria and had watched three software vendors fail in it. Its first product, Sarvatra Mill Core, digitised what a cane yard actually does: the bond, the indent that tells a grower which day to cut, the weighbridge slip, the deduction register and the cane account. By October 2026 it ran in 74 mills across eastern Uttar Pradesh, the Terai, Bihar and, in four sites, western Maharashtra. Annual recurring revenue was ₹40.87 crore. The company employed 214 people.

The decision that shaped everything came in 2018, when Sarvatra had eleven customers and no cash. To win the first cohort of mills, Yogeshwar sold perpetual site licences with an annual maintenance charge instead of subscriptions. Thirty-one of the 74 mills, or 41.9 per cent of the base, still sit on that paper. Clause 7.2 of that contract grants the licensee, at no additional charge, "all present and future functionality forming part of cane accounting, including any successor or replacement thereof."

In 2018 the clause was a concession that cost nothing. In 2026 it meant that whether 31 mills paid for Kanta Live depended not on what the module did but on what Sarvatra called it. If the launch described the module as the completion of cane accounting, those mills received it free, permanently. If it described a payments and compliance service, they paid. Eklavya Upadhyay, the company's counsel, had put it to Shubhangi in September in a sentence she had not stopped thinking about: the launch page was not marketing collateral, it was evidence.

3. Cane, cash and the calendar

Uttar Pradesh crushes more cane than any other state in India, and the commercial relationship between mill and grower is statutory rather than negotiated. The state sets a State Advised Price above the centre's Fair and Remunerative Price; the Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act requires payment to the grower within fourteen days of delivery; the Cane Commissioner's office in Lucknow publishes arrears and can attach a mill's sugar stock. Mills therefore do not experience farmer payment as a service-level question. They experience it as an exposure.

The software market around this is thin. Large integrated groups such as Balrampur Chini Mills, Triveni Engineering and DCM Shriram run substantial in-house cane systems with SAP behind them. The state's own E-Ganna platform gives growers their calendar and slip on a phone, so Sarvatra is never the only screen a farmer sees. At the small end, mills keep cane accounts in Tally and run the yard on registers and WhatsApp. Payment rails are a commodity: UPI and IMPS through NPCI, payouts through Razorpay and the private banks, and the DPDP Act now governing every grower phone number Sarvatra touches.

Sarvatra's exposure runs outward too. Yashodhara Ojha ran customer success from Singapore, where three of the company's trading-house contacts sit, and Hansa Süd Rohstoff GmbH of Hamburg — a raw-sugar buyer that had begun auditing its Indian supply for grower-payment traceability — had asked for a certified data extract by 15 December. Lavanya Nigam, the data scientist who had built the pilot analysis, worked from Toronto on a contract that ended in March, nine and a half hours behind Gorakhpur, which in practice meant her answers arrived after the Indian day had already decided things.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Kanta Live began in November 2024 as an engineering project, not a product. Satyendra Kushwaha's team in Pune built a bridge from the weighbridge slip to a payout instruction, so a mill could pay a grower against a delivery rather than a fortnightly reconciliation, and message the grower the same evening. It was piloted in the 2025-26 season at six mills.

The pilot result, Exhibit 2, was the strongest number the company had ever produced, and it became its belief about itself. Shubhangi wrote the product brief around it in April 2026; Lakshmikant Dubey's team began demonstrating it in May; Yogeshwar quoted it to the board in June.

Ekta Chaubey joined on 1 June 2026 in Bengaluru at ₹46 lakh a year — eight lakh more than Shubhangi, a fact that was known in Gorakhpur and not discussed — with a five-month probation ending 31 October. She spent June and July on the pack Shubhangi wanted. In August she went to the belt, sat in four cane yards, and came back with something that did not fit.

Three things had since turned out to be wrong. The first was the assumption that the grower and the mill wanted the same thing. Exhibit 3 shows that they rank the module's benefits almost in mirror image. The second was the claim itself. The May deck said Kanta Live "pays your growers inside fourteen days", and Exhibit 5 shows that across 6,30,000 deliveries in the first eight weeks of the pilot season, 5,01,925 were paid inside fourteen days, or 79.7 per cent — a good number, and not the claim. The third was that anybody could pick the launch date. Exhibit 6 shows the season notification has come between 12 and 30 October over five years, with the first mill starting between seven and sixteen days later.

In late September a growers' society in Bahraich read the fourteen-day sentence aloud at a meeting with a pilot mill that had fallen behind for reasons unconnected to software. The mill's director rang Lakshmikant, not Ekta.

5. The people

Shubhangi Tripathi, head of product, Gorakhpur, ₹38 lakh. Joined from a Pune SaaS firm in 2023 with its vocabulary intact. Position: the handover pack is the right instrument and should go live on Monday. Incentive: her 2027 roadmap has four modules on it and none of them survive if she personally runs another launch. Not saying: she wrote the fourteen-day sentence.

Ekta Chaubey, product marketing manager, Bengaluru, ₹46 lakh, probation ends 31 October. Position: a handover of a fixed message is the wrong shape; what the company needs is a weekly claim review that she chairs. Incentive: she needs a visible win before 31 October. Not saying: her forty-six field interviews were with buyers, not growers, and she knows the sample is small.

Yogeshwar Pathak, founder, Gorakhpur. Position: whatever gets the module into mills before the first cane is weighed. Incentive: a Series B conversation opening in January that needs a second revenue line. Not saying: he signed clause 7.2 himself and has not told the board what it may cost.

Lakshmikant Dubey, head of sales, Gorakhpur and the road, ₹34 lakh plus commission. Position: give him one sentence and a price and leave him alone until March. Incentive: 70 per cent of his year closes between the notification and Holi. Not saying: two of his reps have already promised the module free to perpetual-licence mills to protect renewals.

Satyendra Kushwaha, engineering lead, Pune. Position: the module does what it says; the failures were mills without money. Incentive: he wants the payout rail counted as infrastructure, not as a launch. Not saying: reconciliation for co-operative mills is three weeks from done.

Lavanya Nigam, data scientist, Toronto, contract to March 2027. Position: the pilot mean is unweighted and fragile, and she has said so twice in writing. Incentive: she wants the analysis re-run before it is quoted again. Not saying: she has never visited a mill.

Yashodhara Ojha, customer success, Singapore. Position: nothing should change for existing mills mid-season. Incentive: her renewal book. Not saying: she has already promised Hansa Süd a traceability extract that the product does not yet produce.

Eklavya Upadhyay, counsel, Bengaluru. Position: no public description of the module may be issued until he has cleared the words against clause 7.2 and the DPDP consent language. Incentive: he carries the downside alone. Not saying: he thinks the fourteen-day sentence is already a representation and is quietly unsure whether removing it now looks worse than leaving it.

7. Voices

"Positioning is not a document you hand over. In this belt it is a thing you say again every Monday, because the reason the mill cares changed on Friday. Give me the pack if you like. By November it is a museum piece."

I built it so that the things which do not change — what the product is, what it cannot do, who pays — stop being renegotiated in every meeting."

— Shubhangi Tripathi, reply, 6 October

"Kindly decide by Dussehra. After the notification I am in a jeep. Whatever is on the one-pager on that day is what all seventy-four mills will hear until March, and I would rather it were written by somebody than by my reps."

"Before anything is published: is this module cane accounting or is it not? I cannot clear one page that says one thing to the perpetual cohort and another to a co-operative tender. Whichever we choose, we will be held to it, and we will be held to it by the party who benefits."

— Eklavya Upadhyay, memorandum, 28 September

"Hamburg has asked for the extract by 15 December and I have said yes. Please do not let the launch decide the word 'traceability' without me."

8. The options as Shubhangi sees them at midnight

A. Ship the handover. Give Ekta the pack on Monday. She owns positioning, messaging, packaging and enablement; Shubhangi keeps the roadmap and a veto on claims. It is clean, it is what the textbook says, and it assumes the message holds still for a season. Exhibit 6 says the season will not hold still for the message.

B. No handover; a standing claim council. Ekta chairs a thirty-minute Monday review with sales, engineering and counsel that reissues the one sentence reps may use that week. It matches the belt. It also means no single person is accountable for the words in a contract dispute, and it asks Eklavya to clear language fifty-two times a year.

C. Split by audience, not by function. Product owns the mill-director story — arrears, working capital, compliance — because that is where clause 7.2 lives. Product marketing owns the grower and society story. Figure 2 shows why this may not survive contact: both stories are read aloud in the same room.

D. Do not launch a named product this season. Ship it quietly inside Mill Core, take the ₹688.00 lakh path, protect renewals and the co-operative tender, and revisit in April. It forfeits ₹496.00 lakh of perpetual-cohort revenue and, Eklavya believes, concedes clause 7.2 permanently.

Ekta's note implies a fifth possibility Shubhangi has not written down: that the question is not who owns positioning but whether Sarvatra has anyone whose job is to keep a claim true as the world moves under it — and that this is neither a product job nor a marketing job as either of them currently understands it.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

  • The Cane Commissioner's notification is expected between 15 and 25 October; first crushing follows in 7 to 16 days (Exhibit 6).
  • Clause 7.2 binds 31 mills, 41.9 per cent of the base, and turns on the word "accounting".
  • The co-operative tender amendment window closed on 30 September; 15 mills are behind it.
  • Launch budget for the season is ₹48.00 lakh, of which ₹11.00 lakh is already committed to print and trade-fair space.
  • The payout rail costs ₹2.50 per instruction; a six-mill season is ₹39.38 lakh, ₹6.56 lakh per mill.
  • Ekta's probation ends 31 October. Lavanya's contract ends in March. Hansa Süd's extract is due 15 December.
  • Every grower phone number is personal data under the DPDP Act, and consent language is unwritten.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 5 come from the same mills in the same season. What claim, if any, can Sarvatra publish that both support?
  2. Panel A and Panel B of Exhibit 3 disagree. Whose answer is "the customer's", and what would you do to find out which sample is misleading you?
  3. Exhibit 4 presents a ₹256.00 lakh gap as though it were the decision. What is it actually hiding, and who in the company benefits from it being read the easy way?
  4. The fourteen-day sentence was written by the head of product and is now quoted back by a growers' society. Who owns a claim that turns out to be wrong in market — the person who wrote it, the person who published it, or the person who must now stand in front of it?
  5. If the reason a buyer cares genuinely changes week by week, what survives a handover at all, and what would you put in Ekta's pack that would still be true in March?
  6. What should Shubhangi do at nine o'clock on Monday morning, and what exactly would she say to the board in January if the season has gone badly?

11. Sunday, 11.50 p.m.

Shubhangi opened the pack to page one, where she had written, in the confident register of her old company, "Positioning owner: Product Marketing. Effective 12 October 2026." Below it, in a comment she had not yet resolved, Ekta had typed: "Effective until when?"

Outside, a tractor-trolley of cane went down Park Road towards a mill that had not yet been told when it could start crushing. Shubhangi looked at the handover pack, then at Lavanya's April footnote, then at the forty-eight WhatsApp messages, and did not move either document into the shared drive.
